simple: a schedule that says who must answer if the system breaks, today and each day after.
analogy: the list on the site office wall: who has the key and the phone this weekend.
precise: a schedule that assigns, for every period, a primary responder (and usually a secondary) who must acknowledge alerts for a service within an agreed time and has the access and knowledge to act; the load it places on people is part of its design.

simple: "I have seen the alarm and I am on it"; if nobody says that in time, the alarm goes to the next person.
analogy: if the foreman does not answer the phone, the call goes to the deputy.
precise: acknowledging a page stops its repetition and records who owns the response; an escalation policy sends an unacknowledged page to the next responder after a set time. In this chapter's model the time is 5 minutes.
source: D1 of F12-16 (pending verification); R2 of F12-16 (runs in this build)

simple: a problem big enough that the team stops normal work and responds together, with roles.
analogy: the moment the foreman says "this is a burst pipe, everybody listen".
precise: an unplanned event that degrades a service below its objectives (or threatens to), formally declared so that roles, a communication channel and a record start; declaring is a decision with a time stamp, not a feeling.

simple: a number that says how bad the incident is, so everybody reacts the same way.
analogy: a dripping tap, a burst pipe, a flooded house.
precise: a team-defined scale (for example SEV1 to SEV4) whose levels are written in advance in terms of user impact (share of requests failing, data at risk, duration) and that sets the response: who is paged, how often stakeholders are updated, whether a post-mortem is required. The levels and their names are local decisions, not a standard.

simple: the one person who runs the response and makes the decisions, without doing the hands-on work.
analogy: the foreman who watches the whole site and holds no tools.
precise: the role that owns an incident from declaration to resolution: assigns the other roles, keeps the current picture, sets priorities (mitigate first), approves changes, decides on escalation and handover, and declares the incident resolved. Every role not delegated stays with the IC.

simple: the only person allowed to change the broken system during the incident.
analogy: the plumber at the valve.
precise: the role that performs (or directs, if several hands are needed) every change to production during the incident, so that changes are serialised, announced before they happen and recorded.

simple: the person who tells everyone outside the response what is going on, regularly.
analogy: the person who phones the owner and the neighbours.
precise: the role that publishes status updates to stakeholders (users, support, management, dependent teams) on a promised schedule and shields the responders from interruptions.

simple: the person who writes down what happened and when, while it happens.
analogy: the site diary.
precise: the role (often called planning or documentation) that keeps the live incident record: timestamps, observations, decisions and who made them, open questions and follow-ups; the record is the first draft of the post-mortem timeline (F12-18).

simple: stopping the harm first, even before you know why it happened.
analogy: closing the main valve before looking for the crack.
precise: an action that ends or reduces user impact without necessarily removing the cause (rolling back, failing over, shedding load, disabling a feature); the fix of the cause comes later. Not the same as a security mitigation (F11-13).

simple: written steps for a known kind of problem, so the person on call does not have to invent them at 3 a.m.
analogy: the laminated card next to the valve: "if water, close this, then call this number".
precise: a document attached to an alert or a failure mode that lists checks, safe actions, their risks and how to verify them; it is code-reviewed and tested like code, and it ages like code.

simple: a guess about the cause, written so that a test can prove it wrong.
analogy: "the leak is at the shower drain": run the shower alone and see.
precise: a statement about the cause of a symptom that predicts an observation not yet made; a useful hypothesis names a test whose result would differ if it were false.

simple: a check whose answer is different depending on which guess is right.
analogy: running only the shower: the stain grows if the shower leaks, stays the same if the bath leaks.
precise: an observation or experiment chosen because the competing hypotheses predict different outcomes for it; a test that every hypothesis predicts the same way carries no information, however long it takes.

simple: lining up the start of a problem with everything that changed shortly before it.
analogy: the stain appeared the day after the shower was fitted.
precise: comparing the onset time of a symptom with the change record (deployments, configuration, traffic, dependencies, scheduled jobs, certificates and other time-based events) to produce candidate causes; it ranks hypotheses, it does not prove them.

simple: splitting requests into those that worked and those that failed and asking what the failed ones have in common.
analogy: which rooms have stains, and what is above each of them?
precise: grouping events by attribute values (node, version, region, size, customer) and comparing failure rates between groups, then within groups, to find the smallest description that covers the failures.
source: R1 of F12-17 (runs in this build)

simple: a hidden third thing that makes an innocent suspect look guilty.
analogy: stains appear under the new bathroom tiles, but the tiles are innocent: the new shower was fitted the same week.
precise: a variable associated with both a candidate cause and the outcome, producing an association between them without causation; controlled by comparing within groups that share the confounder's value.
source: D4 of F12-17 (pending verification); R1 of F12-17 (runs in this build)

simple: finding which version broke something by testing the middle version, then the middle of the half that is still in doubt, and so on.
analogy: closing half the valves, then half of the remaining ones.
precise: binary search over an ordered history (commits, builds, configuration versions) between a known good and a known bad point; it needs about log2(n) tests and a reliable verdict at every step; git bisect automates the bookkeeping.
source: D3 of F12-17 (pending verification); R2 of F12-17 (runs in this build)

simple: for every part of the machine, check how busy it is, whether work is queuing for it, and whether it reports errors.
analogy: for every pipe: how much flows, is water backing up, is anything dripping?
precise: a checklist method for performance and resource problems: for each resource (CPUs, memory, disks, network interfaces, locks, thread pools), check utilisation, saturation and errors.

simple: "how many out of how many", instead of "how many".
analogy: drops per litre of water used, not drops per hour, because nobody showers at night.
precise: a count divided by its denominator over the same window (errors per request, not errors per minute), so that changes in load do not look like changes in health; the SLI of F5-42 is a normalised rate.
source: R3 of F12-17 (runs in this build)

simple: a written story of an incident: what happened, why, and what will change, written after it is over.
analogy: the meeting after the fire drill went wrong.
precise: a document, and the review meeting around it, that records an incident's impact, timeline, causes and contributing factors, detection and response, and action items with owners; written for every incident above an agreed severity and shared so that others can learn from it.

simple: a post-mortem that asks what let the problem happen, not who to punish.
analogy: "what made it possible for sensible people to go to the wrong place?"
precise: a post-mortem written on the assumption that every person acted reasonably given what they knew, the tools they had and the pressure they were under; it describes actions and the conditions that shaped them, and directs its fixes at those conditions. Blameless does not mean without responsibility: owners are named for the fixes.

simple: the event that set the problem off.
analogy: the alarm going off is the trigger of the drill; the moved sign is why it went wrong.
precise: the event or change that started the incident (a deploy, a scheduled job, a traffic peak); it activates latent weaknesses but is rarely the only cause, and removing it alone usually leaves the weakness in place.

simple: after you know how a story ended, the warning signs look obvious, although they were not obvious at the time.
analogy: after the drill, everybody "knew" the sign had moved.
precise: the tendency to judge past decisions with information that was only available afterwards; post-mortems counter it by reconstructing what each person could see at each moment.

simple: a sentence about what did not happen: "if she had…", "he should have…".
analogy: "the carpenters should have taken off their ear protection".
precise: a statement about an alternative past; in a post-mortem it describes a world that did not exist and hides why the real actions made sense at the time; the useful version asks what would have made the better action easy or automatic.

simple: one concrete change, with a person who owns it and a date.
analogy: "put an arrow on the sign and a light on the alarm by next Monday, Juma".
precise: a tracked work item arising from a post-mortem, typed by what it does (prevent the trigger or weakness, detect it sooner, mitigate its impact, or change a process), with an owner, a due date and a priority; "be more careful" is not an action item.

simple: a picture of many safety layers, each with holes; an accident happens when the holes line up.
analogy: the sign, the alarm and the headcount were three layers; this month each had a hole in the same place.
precise: a model of accident causation in which defences (technical, procedural, organisational) are imperfect barriers with latent and active failures; an incident passes through when weaknesses in several layers coincide, so prevention strengthens layers rather than searching for one culprit.

simple: asking "why?" again and again to get from the symptom to deeper causes.
analogy: why did people go to the wrong place? Why was the sign moved? Why was there no announcement?
precise: an iterative questioning technique for causal analysis; useful to get past the first answer, but a single chain of whys forces one cause per level and tends to stop at a person, so post-mortems use it as a prompt, not as the method.

simple: something that almost went wrong, and did not, this time.
analogy: the carpenters came out after four minutes; nobody was hurt.
precise: an event, or a period inside an incident, in which a further failure would have caused (more) harm; recorded under "where we got lucky", because it shows a weakness at no cost.

simple: the official report written by the people who investigated a failure.
analogy: the inspector's forty pages, not the café story.
precise: the document published by the body that investigated an accident or failure (an inquiry board, a safety agency, an audit office, the organisation's own published post-mortem); for the facts of that event it is the primary source, ranked above papers about it, which rank above news and retellings (guide tiers 1, 5 and 6 respectively).
source: D7 of F12-19 (the project authoring guide)

simple: what the investigators concluded, and what they said should change.
analogy: "the bracket was rated for the old snow tables" and "drawings must name the tables they use".
precise: a finding is a conclusion the report draws from its evidence (often numbered and classified as cause or contributing factor); a recommendation is an action the report proposes to an addressee; quoting a report means quoting its findings and recommendations as findings and recommendations, with their numbers.
source: D7 of F12-19 (the project authoring guide)

simple: a kind of mistake that keeps happening in different systems.
analogy: "load rated for old tables" can happen to roofs, floors and bridges.
precise: a mechanism of failure abstracted from particular incidents (a numeric conversion out of range, a unit mismatch at an interface, time accumulated in a finite representation, a race between concurrent activities) for which detection and prevention techniques can be stated independently of any one system.
source: R1, R3, R4 of F12-19 (runs in this build)

simple: putting a number into a smaller box, where big values do not fit.
analogy: pouring a large bucket into a small jug.
precise: a conversion to a type that cannot represent all values of the source type; in C++, converting a floating value whose integer part does not fit the destination integer type is undefined behaviour, and converting an integer to a narrower signed integer type is, since C++20, defined as reduction modulo 2N.
source: D5 of F12-19 (pending verification); R1 of F12-19 (runs in this build)

simple: a type that says what a number means, so mixing meanings stops the build.
analogy: a measuring tape labelled "centimetres only".
precise: a distinct type wrapping a value (for example struct NewtonSeconds { double value; };) so that the compiler rejects passing one quantity or unit where another is expected; conversions become explicit functions.
source: R4 of F12-19 (runs in this build)

simple: a tiny error, repeated millions of times, that grows into a large one.
analogy: a ruler one hair too short, used to measure a long road.
precise: the error that builds up when a value that is not exactly representable (such as 0.1 in binary) is added or stored repeatedly; it grows with the number of operations (for example with uptime) and depends on the representation's precision.
source: D6 of F12-19 (pending verification); R3 of F12-19 (runs in this build)

simple: checking your own work for the same kind of mistake someone else made.
analogy: "do we build roofs like that?"
precise: the step that turns a documented failure into local action: name the failure class, search your systems for it with a stated method (a compiler warning, a code search, a test), record what was found, and add a check that keeps it from coming back.
